question: How does a dog smell so much better than I do?
teaser: Open a dog's nose, follow the air to its smell lining, and meet the cell that catches an odour and the brain's first stop.

stops.title: A dog in the park
text: A dog lives in a world of smells. This model is a typical medium-sized dog about 57 centimetres tall at the shoulder and about 30 kilograms. Her nose does two jobs, breathing and smelling, and it keeps them partly apart. Most of the smelling is done far inside.
stops.model: A procedural model of a typical dog, not one breed.
stops.notice: Look at the bare, moist tip of the nose.

stops.title: Two paths for the air

do.press: Turn the cut to face me

text: Air that a dog breathes in does not all go the same way. Most of it passes the scrolls at the front, which warm and moisten it, and goes on towards the lungs. A smaller share is steered up a narrow path to a pocket at the back of the nose, called the olfactory recess, where thin scrolls of bone covered with a smell-sensing lining are folded like parchment. In a computer model built from a scan of one dog, about 12 to 13 percent of the air breathed in reached that smell region.
stops.model: A model of the inside of a dog's nose built for this world. The folds are typical, not copied from one animal, and the real folding is much finer.
stops.notice: Find the scrolls at the back (smell) and the scrolls at the front (airway).

stops.title: Sniffing

do.press: Turn the cut to face me

text: A sniffing dog takes about 4 to 7 short sniffs every second, roughly ten times faster than a person sniffs. The air she breathes out leaves by a different route, a jet from the side of the nose, and it mostly bypasses the smell pocket. So the odour-laden air in the pocket is held there, and the odour has more time to reach the lining.
stops.model: A model of the inside of a dog's nose built for this world. The airflow itself is not drawn.
stops.notice: Compare the pocket at the back with the open airway scrolls in front of it.

stops.title: How much lining
text: A dog's smell lining covers about 170 square centimetres in the figure usually quoted, against about 5 to 10 in a person. The area depends on the breed and size of the dog, and old measurements differ. A dog also has more working types of smell receptor: about 800 working receptor genes against about 400 in a person, counted from genome studies.
stops.model: The dog's lining area comes from an encyclopedia figure and varies with breed. Gene counts depend on how a working gene is defined.
stops.notice: Compare the numbers: the area differs by roughly ten to forty times, the number of receptor types by about two.

do.press: Turn the cut to face me

stops.title: The smell cell
text: Smell cells are nerve cells. Each has a tuft of tiny hairs, called cilia, in the mucus at the surface. When an odour molecule fits a receptor on one of these hairs, the cell sends a signal along its thread to the brain. Each smell cell carries just one kind of receptor, so the brain can tell odours apart by which cells fire.
stops.model: An illustration of the layers of the smell lining. It shows the kinds of cell and their order, not a micrograph, and sizes are simplified.
stops.notice: Click a smell cell and then the thread that leaves it.

stops.title: The brain's first stop
text: Every smell cell sends its thread to one of two olfactory bulbs at the front of the brain. In the bulb, cells with the same kind of receptor send their threads to the same small clusters, so each cluster answers to one kind of odour molecule. From there the signal goes on to the rest of the brain.
How much of a dog's skill comes from its nose, its receptors or how its brain reads the signal is not settled.
stops.model: The bulbs are drawn in a model of a typical dog, not a scan of one animal.
stops.notice: Find the two knobs at the front of the brain.

stops.title: And in you
text: A person has the same kind of smell lining, high in the nose. It covers about 5 to 10 square centimetres and uses about 400 working receptor genes. A person has no olfactory recess, so the smell lining sits on the main path of the breath, and a person sniffs about ten times slower than a dog. People still smell well, so the difference is one of degree.
stops.notice: Open the card for the human nose and compare it with the dog's: it is the same kind of organ, smaller, and without the separate pocket.

answer: A dog smells better because its nose steers a share of each sniffed breath into a separate pocket, lined with a much larger area of smell cells that have about twice as many kinds of receptor, and because it sniffs fast and breathes out by another route so odour stays in the pocket. A person has the same kind of lining on a smaller patch, on the main airway.
unknown: How much of the difference comes from the nose, the receptors and the brain is still debated, and the number of smell cells in a dog is only an old estimate that differs between sources.
sources: Airflow, olfactory recess, 12 to 13 percent of inspired air, sniffing 4 to 7 Hz in dogs of 6.8 to 52.9 kg against 0.3 to 0.7 Hz in people, expired jet, region area about 200 cm2: Craven, Paterson and Settles 2010, J R Soc Interface 7:933, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2871809
Smell lining about 170 cm2 in the dog and 5 to 10 cm2 in people: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Chemoreception: Smell (as reported by a search; page not fetched), and card dog_turb_olf

Receptor genes: Quignon et al. 2005 (dog about 1,094 olfactory receptor genes, about 20 percent pseudogenes) and Gilad et al. 2005 Genome Research 15:224 (human: 862 genes, 56 percent disrupted); about 800 against about 400 working genes is my rounding of these
